title: Test-driven development: the search function
summary: The test-driven development loop, writing a failing test for search, why the signature needs a lifetime, making the test pass with lines and contains, and wiring search into run.

sections: TRPL 12.4 Adding Functionality with Test-Driven Development
TRPL 12.4 Writing Code to Pass the Test
TRPL 12.4 Iterating Through Lines with the lines Method
TRPL 12.4 Searching Each Line for the Query
TRPL 12.4 Using the search Function in the run Function

blocks.md:
With the logic in `lib.rs`, it can be tested. Write the search itself using **test-driven development** (TDD), a loop of four steps:

1. Write a test that fails, and run it to make sure it fails **for the reason you expect**.
2. Write or change just enough code to make the new test pass.
3. Refactor the code you just added, and check the tests still pass.
4. Repeat.

TDD is one of many ways to write software, but it keeps test coverage high and makes you design the function's interface from the caller's side first.

blocks.title: 1. A failing test
blocks.md: The test says what `search` should do: given a query and some text, return the lines containing the query.

blocks.explain: The backslash after the opening quote tells Rust not to put a newline at the start of the literal. `unimplemented!()` (like `todo!()`) panics, so the test compiles and fails.

blocks.title: Why the lifetime 'a?
blocks.md: `search` returns slices of `contents`, not of `query`. The signature says exactly that: the returned `&'a str` values live as long as `contents`. Without the annotation, Rust cannot tell which argument the result borrows from (chapter 10, error E0106). With it, a caller may drop `query` and keep the results.

blocks.code:
$ cargo test
running 1 test
test tests::one_result ... FAILED

failures:

---- tests::one_result stdout ----

thread 'tests::one_result' panicked at src/lib.rs:2:5:
not implemented
blocks.explain: It fails, and for the expected reason. Step 1 done.

blocks.title: 2. Make it pass
blocks.md: The function needs to go through each line, check whether it contains the query, and collect those that do. `str` has a method for each step: **`lines()`** iterates over lines (handling `\n` and `\r\n`), and **`contains()`** checks for a substring.

blocks.explain: The test passes. Step 3 (refactor) comes in chapter 13, where iterator adapters shorten this to one expression.

blocks.title: Using search in run

blocks.code:
$ cargo run -- frog poem.txt
How public, like a frog

$ cargo run -- body poem.txt
I'm nobody! Who are you?
Are you nobody, too?
How dreary to be somebody!

$ cargo run -- monomorphization poem.txt
$
blocks.explain: One match, several matches, and no matches. minigrep works.

blocks.title: TDD: line numbers
blocks.md: Real grep can print line numbers (`grep -n`). The assertions in `main` describe `search_numbered`, which returns `(line_number, line)` pairs, counting from 1. They fail now; make them pass. Hint: `enumerate()` yields `(index, item)` pairs.
blocks.task: Make the assertions pass so the program prints `2: safe, fast, productive.`

questions.q: In `fn search<'a>(query: &str, contents: &'a str) -> Vec<&'a str>`, the results borrow from...
questions.explanation: Each result is a line of contents.

questions.q: Why run the new test before writing the code?
options: To check it fails, and fails for the reason you expect, so it really tests something
questions.explanation: A test that never failed may not test anything.

points: TDD: failing test, minimal code to pass, refactor, repeat.
`search` returns slices of `contents`, so its signature ties the result to `contents` with `'a`.
`lines()` and `contains()` do the work; results go into a `Vec<&str>`.
